laws.rule: Penalties for drug offences are severe. They include fines and long prison sentences in local jails. Pack your luggage yourself. Don't carry anything through customs for anyone else. US authorities may do thorough drug searches in The Bahamas.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: Serious crimes can attract the death penalty, including: aggravated murder terrorism treason war crimes The legal age for same-sex relations is 18.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: To drive in The Bahamas, you'll need both: a valid Australian driver's licence (digital driver's licences may not be accepted) an International Driving Permit (IDP) You must get your IDP before leaving Australia.
laws.heading: Driving permit

laws.rule: All drones must be registered with the Civil Aviation Authority Bahamas, including a visitor's. For a drone over 249 g the visitor attaches the home-country registration or certificate, a passport photo page scan, arrival and departure dates and the island of use. CAA-B says it needs at least five business days; the authorisation covers arrival to departure dates. A recreational registration fee of US$30 (US$50 expedited) is listed. Customs has its own rules for drones.
laws.heading: Drone registration for visitors

laws.rule: Each traveller (or the responsible family member) must declare cash or negotiable instruments, precious metals or stones worth B$10,000 or more (B$ is at par with US$; US$10,000 is about A$14,200, RBA 30 Oct 2026: A$1 = USD 0.7040). The rule is aimed at money laundering and tax evasion.
laws.penalty_signal: Forfeiture of the cash, plus a fine of up to B$2,000

laws.rule: Duty-free allowance for adults: up to one quart of spirits and one quart of wine; tobacco up to one pound by weight, or 200 cigarettes, or 50 cigars. Visitors also have a B$100 exemption on other dutiable goods.
All food products must be declared. Fruit, vegetables and some dairy are restricted to protect plant and animal health.
laws.penalty_signal: Failure to declare can lead to forfeiture or fines

drone-pilot-pathway.summary: CAA-B authorises commercial drone work case by case by written approval; no public register of operators was found on the pages read. Visitors register drones through CAA-B.

items.text: No public list of approved commercial drone operators was found on the CAA-B drone pages read.

Commercial drone operations need written approval from CAA-B before they start. The application asks for insurance, drone registration from the home country, a map, WGS84 coordinates, flight height and local representative details. CAA-B sets the fee after reviewing the application. No pilot-licence level is stated on the page.

The commercial form asks for the applicant's nationality and the state or country of registration of the drone, so foreign applicants are contemplated; CAA-B asks for a handling agency or local representative where applicable. Drone work without prior written approval is stated as prohibited.
Visitors register a drone with CAA-B before arrival; CAA-B says it needs at least five business days. The Bahamas Customs Department has its own rules for bringing a drone in.
